gloss_terse: parched, dried out from thirst or heat
gloss_readable: This adjective intensifies the idea of being completely dried out, going beyond ordinary thirst to extreme desiccation. Isaiah uses it to describe people so parched with thirst that they are dying (Isa 5:13). The Spanish 'reseca' captures the sense of thorough drying, while the English 'parched-of' shows the construction with the following noun.

senses.1: Describes the state of being extremely dried out or desiccated, especially from lack of water. Isaiah 5:13 depicts the exile's severity: people 'parched with thirst,' showing complete dehydration. This intensive adjective form (note BDB's citation of Gesenius §84b-c) emphasizes the extremity of the condition, not merely thirsty but utterly withered.

gloss_readable: This verb describes brilliant whiteness or dazzling appearance, particularly of skin. The Syriac cognate suggests brightness and clarity, while the Aramaic points to polishing. In Lamentations 4:7, it describes the Nazirites' radiant appearance before Jerusalem's fall—their skin 'more dazzling than milk,' whiter than snow. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'eran blancos,' English 'bright') confirms this sense of brilliant whiteness.

senses.1: To appear dazzlingly white or brilliant. Lamentations 4:7 uses this to describe the Nazirites' complexion before the siege: 'more dazzling than milk,' parallel to 'whiter than snow.' The verb emphasizes radiant, gleaming whiteness rather than mere color, suggesting skin that shone with health and vigor in contrast to their later emaciated state.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes land that has been scorched or parched by heat. The root suggests extreme dryness, beyond what rain can relieve. Psalm 68:6 uses it to describe the desolate places where God settles the rebellious. The Spanish 'sequedad' and French 'terre desséchée' both capture the sense of thoroughly dried earth, land too parched to support life.

senses.1: Land that is scorched and dried to the point of desolation. Psalm 68:6 describes God making rebels dwell 'in a parched land,' suggesting barren desert as both geographical reality and divine judgment. This goes beyond normal aridity to describe earth burned and hardened, inhospitable to human habitation.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a repulsive odor, particularly of decay. Joel 2:20 uses it in parallel with another word for stench to describe the smell of the invading northern army when God drives it away. The doubling of stench-words ('his foul smell' parallel to 'his stench') emphasizes the complete putrefaction of the defeated horde. French 'puanteur' directly captures this sense of repulsive smell.

senses.1: A foul, nauseating smell, especially of rotting organic matter. Joel 2:20 depicts God's judgment on the invading army: 'his foul smell will rise up,' paralleled by 'his stench.' The imagery suggests corpses decomposing in the sun, a graphic picture of total defeat. The Siracide reference (11:12) also uses it for offensive odor.

gloss_readable: This plural noun describes areas of extreme drought or scorched land. Isaiah 58:11 uses it in God's promise to satisfy His people's needs even in the driest places. The root connects to scorching heat and parched ground. The Spanish 'sequías' (droughts) and the broader context of divine provision in waterless places show this refers to regions where water is desperately scarce.

senses.1: Scorched or drought-stricken regions where water is absent and the ground is parched. Isaiah 58:11 contains God's promise: 'He will satisfy your needs in scorched places,' assuring provision even in the most barren environments. This builds on the root idea of land dried by intense heat, emphasizing not just aridity but the burning, scorched quality of the terrain.

gloss_terse: reddish-gray, tawny (of wool or possibly a place name)
gloss_readable: This noun appears to describe either a color of wool or possibly a place name. The primary sense is reddish-gray or tawny wool mentioned in Ezekiel 27:18's catalog of Damascus's trading goods. Some scholars suggest it might be 'wool from Zahar' (a location), though this is disputed. The color term fits the context of luxury trade items, while translations vary between 'white' (Spanish, French) and the more technical 'tawny' suggested by BDB.

senses.1: A reddish-gray or tawny color, specifically describing wool in the luxury trade of Damascus (Ezekiel 27:18). The exact shade is debated—BDB suggests 'tawny' or 'reddish-gray,' while some translations opt for 'white.' The multilingual evidence shows uncertainty, but the context of fine trade goods suggests a distinctive, valuable color of wool, possibly from a specific region or processing method.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes the color of donkeys, appearing only in Judges 5:10 in Deborah's song. The root relates to colors in the reddish, tawny, or light spectrum. The phrase 'you who ride on tawny donkeys' addresses the wealthy or ruling class, since lighter-colored donkeys were apparently prized. Spanish 'blancas' (white) and the English retention of 'tawny' show the range of interpretation, but the sense is clearly a desirable, distinctive coloring.

senses.1: Describes a tawny or light coloring of donkeys, suggesting animals of higher value. Judges 5:10 addresses 'you who sit on tawny donkeys,' apparently referring to leaders or the wealthy class. The specific color marked status or breeding quality. The root connects to reddish-gray or tan hues, distinguishing these animals from common darker donkeys.

gloss_readable: This plural noun refers to those who hunt, derived from the root for hunting or trapping. Jeremiah 16:16 uses it in a striking metaphor: God will send first fishermen, then hunters to seek out the exiled Israelites. The hunters represent the thoroughness of God's pursuit—no hiding place will suffice. The multilingual glosses uniformly render it 'hunters,' confirming the straightforward occupational sense.

senses.1: People who hunt or trap animals, used metaphorically in Jeremiah 16:16 for divine agents pursuing scattered Israel. God declares He will send 'many hunters' to search out His people from every hiding place. The image suggests relentless pursuit and thorough searching, moving beyond the fishermen's nets to the hunters' tracking skills in mountains and rocks.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes an instrument of punishment and public humiliation, likely a wooden collar or stocks that restrained prisoners. Jeremiah 29:26 mentions it alongside 'stocks' as tools for restraining mad prophets. The context shows it was used by authorities to control and shame those deemed troublemakers. Spanish 'argolla' (ring, collar) points to the restraining function, while the parallel term confirms it was a device for physical constraint.

senses.1: A restraining device, probably a collar or pillory used to punish and publicly shame prisoners. Jeremiah 29:26 describes the temple officer's authority to put any madman who prophesies 'in the pillory and collar,' showing it was paired with stocks for maximum restraint and humiliation. The device both restricted movement and marked the wearer as condemned.

gloss_terse: Zior, a town in the hill country of Judah
gloss_readable: This proper noun identifies a town in the hill country near Hebron, listed among Judah's inheritance in Joshua 15:54. Modern identification places it at Ṣâʿîr, about five miles north-northeast of Hebron according to Buhl's geography. The Septuagint renders it variously as Σωρθ or Σιωρ. The multilingual glosses preserve the name in transliteration, reflecting its status as a geographical designation.

senses.1: A town name in the tribal allotment of Judah (Joshua 15:54), located in the hill country region. Geographical sources identify it with modern Ṣâʿîr near Hebron. The name appears in the territorial lists defining Judah's inheritance, one of many settlements in the central highlands that formed the tribe's core territory.

gloss_readable: This noun's meaning is debated, but the most common interpretation is 'wings' in the collective sense. Jeremiah 48:9 contains the difficult phrase 'give wings to Moab,' which most scholars understand as a call for Moab to flee swiftly, as if on wings. The Aramaic cognate means wing or fin, supporting this interpretation. However, the Septuagint's 'markers' led some to suggest 'signpost,' and Perles proposed reading 'feathers.' The wing interpretation fits the flight imagery of the context.

senses.1: Wings or wing-feathers, used in the metaphorical command 'give wings to Moab' (Jeremiah 48:9), meaning let Moab flee swiftly. The Aramaic cognates support the 'wing' interpretation, fitting the context of rapid escape from judgment. Though some scholars suggest alternative readings ('signpost' or 'feathers'), the wing imagery best captures the urgency of flight from divine destruction.

gloss_terse: Ziz, the name of an ascent near the Dead Sea
gloss_readable: This place name appears in 2 Chronicles 20:16, referring to an ascent or pass used by invading armies approaching from the Dead Sea region. The 'ascent of Ziz' was the route by which Moabites and Ammonites came up against Jehoshaphat. Buhl's geography identifies it with Wady Ḥaṣâṣâ and the plateau Ḥaṣâṣâ north of En-gedi. The Septuagint renderings vary, but the location is clearly a recognized geographical feature in Judean topography.

senses.1: The name of a mountain pass or ascent near the Dead Sea (2 Chronicles 20:16), by which invading forces approached Judah from the east. Modern scholars connect it with terrain north of En-gedi. The name marks a strategic route through the wilderness, used by armies moving from the Dead Sea basin up into the Judean highlands.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a flower or blossom, appearing in Isaiah 28:4 in construct form. The verse speaks of 'the fading flower' of Ephraim's glory, using floral imagery to depict something beautiful but transient. The Spanish 'flor' (flower) aligns with this botanical sense, while English 'fading' captures the adjective but not the noun itself. The reference note indicates this is the same root as the more common word for flower or blossom.

senses.1: A blossom or flower, used metaphorically in Isaiah 28:4 for the fading glory of Ephraim. The prophet depicts the northern kingdom's splendor as 'the fading flower of its glorious beauty,' emphasizing impermanence. The floral image stresses vulnerability—what blooms brightly soon withers, just as Israel's pride would wilt under Assyrian invasion.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes the pivot or hinge on which a door turns. Proverbs 26:14 uses it in a vivid simile comparing a sluggard turning in bed to a door turning on its hinge—both rotate in place without going anywhere. The image perfectly captures futile activity: much motion, no progress. The Spanish 'gozne' preserves this technical meaning of the hardware that allows rotational movement.

senses.1: The pivot or hinge mechanism that allows a door to swing open and closed. Proverbs 26:14 employs memorable imagery: 'As a door turns on its hinge, so a sluggard turns on his bed.' The comparison highlights purposeless rotation—the door swings but stays in its frame, just as the lazy person rolls over without rising. The hinge becomes a symbol of motion without progress.

gloss_terse: to take provisions, supply oneself with food for a journey
gloss_readable: This denominative verb from the noun for 'provisions' means to supply oneself with food or take provisions for a journey. Joshua 9:4 and 9:12 use it of the Gibeonites' deception—they claimed to have provisioned themselves long ago for a distant journey, showing worn-out bread as proof. The verb appears in Hithpael, suggesting a reflexive action: they supplied themselves. The multilingual glosses show confusion (English 'disguised,' Spanish 'made themselves ambassadors'), but the root sense is taking provisions.

senses.1: To supply oneself with provisions or take food for a journey. Joshua 9:4, 12 uses this verb (in Hithpael) to describe the Gibeonites' claim: 'this bread we took as our provision' when leaving home, allegedly weeks ago. The verb emphasizes the act of preparing travel food. Textual variants suggest v. 4 should also read this verb rather than 'disguised themselves,' maintaining consistency with the provision theme.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a type of cooking vessel, appearing in 2 Chronicles 35:13's description of cooking Passover offerings. It's listed alongside other cooking containers like pots and cauldrons. The context shows various vessels were used to cook the sacrificial meat quickly and distribute it to the people. Spanish 'tazones' (bowls or pans) and the listing with other cookware confirm this is a utilitarian vessel for food preparation.

senses.1: A pot or pan used for cooking, mentioned in the Passover preparations of 2 Chronicles 35:13. The text describes cooking the holy offerings 'in pots, in caldrons, and in pans,' showing these were different sizes or types of cooking vessels. The plural form suggests these were standard equipment for large-scale food preparation during festivals.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes a small jar or container, appearing in 2 Kings 2:20 when Elisha asks for 'a new jar' to hold salt for purifying Jericho's water. The specification of 'new' suggests ceremonial importance—an unused vessel for a miraculous act. The jar needed to be small enough to hold salt but significant enough to be specified in the narrative. This differs from larger storage jars, being more portable and purpose-specific.

senses.1: A jar or small container, specifically mentioned in Elisha's miracle at Jericho (2 Kings 2:20). Elisha requests 'a new jar' to hold salt for purifying the poisoned spring. The newness emphasized ritual purity for the miracle. This was a modest-sized vessel, easily brought to the prophet, suitable for holding a portion of salt—practical but also symbolically important as the container for God's healing agent.

gloss_readable: This verb means to sink or be submerged, especially in water. Exodus 15:10 uses it in the Song of the Sea, describing how Pharaoh's army 'sank like lead in the mighty waters' when God blew His breath over them. The simile emphasizes speed and finality—lead drops straight down without floating. Cognates in other Semitic languages include ideas of sinking to rest or launching (Assyrian), and both sinking and floating (Ethiopic), showing semantic range around water motion.

senses.1: To sink down or be submerged in water, used of Pharaoh's army in Exodus 15:10: 'they sank like lead in the mighty waters.' The verb captures the swift, irreversible downward plunge of the Egyptian forces when the sea returned. The lead simile stresses weight and speed—no struggling or floating, just immediate submersion and death. This became one of Israel's central images of divine deliverance.

gloss_terse: Hazelelponi, a female name in Judah's genealogy
gloss_readable: This proper name belongs to a woman in Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 4:3). The etymology suggests 'give shade, O you who turn to me' or similar, though interpretations vary. The Septuagint offers very different renderings, indicating textual uncertainty. As a feminine name appearing in genealogical lists, it preserves memory of a woman significant enough to be recorded in Judah's family records, though nothing further is known of her.

senses.1: A woman's name appearing in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:3). The name's meaning is uncertain but may relate to 'shade' and 'turning,' possibly 'give shade, O one who turns to me.' The Septuagint's widely variant readings suggest scribal difficulty with the text. This rare feminine name in patriarchal genealogies indicates she held some significance in her family's memory.

gloss_terse: Zalmon, one of David's mighty warriors
gloss_readable: This proper name identifies one of David's elite warriors listed in 2 Samuel 23:28. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:29 calls him Ilai, suggesting either a different name for the same person or a textual variant. The Septuagint renderings also vary. Zalmon appears among the 'thirty' mighty men who formed David's special forces, distinguished warriors with individual recognition for their exploits.

senses.1: A personal name borne by one of David's elite thirty warriors (2 Samuel 23:28). The parallel 1 Chronicles 11:29 gives his name as Ilai, possibly reflecting different traditions or name variants for this fighter. He's listed among the heroes who formed David's core military leadership, each renowned for individual acts of valor in Israel's early monarchy.

gloss_terse: Zalaph, father of a wall-builder under Nehemiah
gloss_readable: This proper name identifies the father of one of Jerusalem's wall-builders in Nehemiah 3:30. The name may derive from a word for caper-plant, according to rabbinic Hebrew. Zalaph's son participated in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls after the exile, and his inclusion in the detailed roster of builders shows he was part of the reconstituted community. The Septuagint preserves the name with typical Greek adaptations.

senses.1: A personal name, the father of one of Nehemiah's wall-builders (Nehemiah 3:30). The name possibly means 'caper-plant' based on later Hebrew usage. Though Zalaph himself isn't described, his son's participation in the wall-rebuilding project marks the family as returnees committed to Jerusalem's restoration. The detailed builder list preserves these names as a memorial of post-exilic faithfulness.

gloss_readable: This place name appears in 1 Samuel 10:2, where Samuel tells Saul he will meet two men 'at Zelzah on Benjamin's border' by Rachel's tomb. However, the text is likely corrupt—scholars note the location is uncertain, and some propose reading 'from Zelah' (another Benjamin town) instead. The Septuagint offers variant readings. Despite textual difficulties, the narrative presents it as a landmark Saul would recognize near Rachel's burial site.

senses.1: A place name in Benjamin mentioned in 1 Samuel 10:2, where Samuel predicts Saul will encounter two men near Rachel's tomb. The location is uncertain—scholars note probable textual corruption, with suggestions to read 'from Zelah' (cf. 2 Samuel 21:14) instead. The name functions in Samuel's prophetic sign to Saul, marking a specific location along his journey home after anointing, though its exact identification remains disputed.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes the whirring or buzzing sound made by rapidly moving wings, particularly of insects. Isaiah 18:1 describes 'the land of whirring wings,' likely referring to either Ethiopia or a region with abundant swarming insects. The construct phrase 'whirring of wings' creates an auditory image of countless flying insects. This onomatopoetic word captures the distinctive humming sound of dense insect populations, though interpreters debate whether it's literal (locusts, flies) or symbolic.

senses.1: The whirring or buzzing sound produced by insect wings in flight. Isaiah 18:1 speaks of 'the land of the whirring of wings,' generally understood as describing a region characterized by swarming insects—perhaps the upper Nile with its abundant flies. The word is onomatopoetic, capturing the distinctive hum of countless wings beating rapidly. Whether literal or symbolic, it evokes an atmosphere thick with flying creatures.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a weapon used for spearing large fish or sea creatures, appearing in Job 40:31 (English 41:7) in God's challenge about capturing Leviathan. The question 'Can you fill his skin with harpoons?' emphasizes the creature's invulnerability to normal fishing weapons. The etymology connects to 'whizzing' or 'whirring,' suggesting the spear's sound in flight. This is specialized equipment for hunting large aquatic prey, distinct from nets or hooks.

senses.1: A spear or harpoon designed for hunting fish or sea creatures. Job 40:31 (41:7 English) asks rhetorically whether anyone can fill Leviathan's hide 'with harpoons,' emphasizing the futility of attacking this monster with conventional weapons. The word derives from the sound the spear makes when thrown—a whizzing or whirring. This was specialized hunting gear for large fish, showing humanity's powerlessness against God's ultimate creation.

gloss_readable: This noun identifies a type of locust or cricket, named for the whirring sound it makes. Deuteronomy 28:42 lists it among covenant curses: 'the whirring locust will possess all your trees and crops.' The cognates in Akkadian and Aramaic also denote chirping or whirring insects. While the exact species is uncertain, the defining characteristic is the sound—a persistent, pervasive noise accompanying agricultural devastation. This is one of several Hebrew locust terms, each perhaps distinguishing types or life stages.

senses.1: A type of locust or cricket characterized by its whirring or buzzing sound, mentioned in Deuteronomy 28:42 as a curse that will 'take possession of all your trees and produce.' The name derives from the distinctive noise these insects make in swarms. Cognate terms in related languages confirm the auditory identification. As a covenant curse, this insect represents comprehensive agricultural destruction, stripping fields bare while filling the air with incessant sound.

gloss_terse: parched condition, state of being dried out from thirst
gloss_readable: This noun describes the parched condition of the throat from thirst, appearing in Jeremiah 2:25 in God's rebuke of Israel's spiritual adultery. God warns, 'Keep your throat from being parched,' meaning stop your frenzied pursuit of foreign gods. The imagery is physical—a throat raw from desperate panting after lovers—but the meaning is spiritual. The dried, parched state symbolizes both the exhausting nature of idolatry and its ultimate inability to satisfy.

senses.1: The parched, dried-out condition of the throat from thirst. Jeremiah 2:25 uses it figuratively: God tells wayward Israel to 'spare your throat from being parched' (from running after other gods). The physical image is vivid—throat raw from panting in desperate pursuit—but applied to spiritual adultery. Israel exhausts herself chasing false lovers, leaving her throat parched and desperate, yet refuses to return to the true source of refreshment.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes a cover or lid for a vessel, appearing in Numbers 19:15's purity regulations. Any open container without a fastened cover in a tent with a corpse becomes unclean. The law required vessels to be sealed or lidded to prevent corpse defilement. The word emphasizes the fastening or binding aspect—the cover must be secured, not just placed on top, to provide effective ritual protection from death's contaminating influence.

senses.1: A cover or lid for a vessel, specifically one that is fastened or tied down. Numbers 19:15 legislates corpse impurity: 'any open vessel which has no cover fastened on it is unclean.' The context is ritual purity—only sealed containers were protected from defilement by a corpse in the same tent. The fastening detail matters: loose covers provided no protection; the lid had to be bound on to create an effective seal against contamination.

gloss_readable: This verb means to dry up or shrivel, appearing in Hosea 9:14's bitter prayer regarding Israel's judgment. The prophet asks God to give Ephraim 'shriveling breasts' incapable of nursing—a devastating image of barrenness and failed motherhood. The parallel phrase 'miscarrying womb' reinforces the theme of generation cut off. The verb captures the withering of what should provide life and nourishment, biological language for national extinction.

senses.1: To dry up, shrivel, or wither, used in Hosea 9:14 in a grim prayer about Israel's judgment: 'give them shriveling breasts' unable to nurse. The verb describes mammary glands drying up, failing their life-giving function. Paired with 'miscarrying womb,' this creates an image of complete reproductive failure—children either lost before birth or starving after. The physical withering symbolizes the nation's future withering under divine judgment.

gloss_readable: This noun likely refers to hooks or barbs, possibly fishing hooks, mentioned in Amos 4:2. The prophet declares that enemies will drag the people of Samaria away 'with hooks,' using fishing imagery for deportation. Parallel to 'fishhooks' in the same verse, this term may distinguish types of hooks or emphasize the totality—every method of catching fish applied to catching people. The Spanish 'ganchos' (hooks) aligns with this interpretation of sharp, barbed instruments for dragging captives.

senses.1: Hooks or barbs used for catching or dragging, appearing in Amos 4:2's prophecy against Samaria's wealthy women. God declares the days are coming when 'they will take you away with hooks,' using fishing metaphors for military deportation. Paired with another term for fishhooks, this creates an image of captives hooked and dragged like fish from water. The barbed implements ensure no escape—brutal and degrading treatment fitting the prophet's judgment oracle.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes coolness or cold, appearing in Proverbs 25:13's simile about a faithful messenger. He is 'like the coolness of snow at harvest time'—refreshing, invigorating, unexpected relief. In the Middle Eastern context, snow-cooled water during the hot harvest season was an extraordinary luxury. The comparison highlights how a reliable messenger brings revitalizing relief to those who send him, as welcome as cold in oppressive heat.

senses.1: Coolness or cold, specifically in the phrase 'coolness of snow' (Proverbs 25:13). The verse compares a trustworthy messenger to 'the coolness of snow at harvest time,' when refreshment is most needed and appreciated. The cold of snow during hot harvest work was both rare and reviving. The image captures how a faithful servant brings psychological and practical refreshment to his masters, renewing their spirits like a cold drink in heat.

gloss_readable: This participle describes something dried up or withered, used in Genesis 41:23 of grain in Pharaoh's dream. The dream features seven thin, wind-blasted ears of grain, described as 'withered'—dried out and incapable of bearing seed. The Aramaic cognate means 'stone,' suggesting hardening through desiccation. These withered ears symbolized seven years of famine that would consume Egypt's abundance, grain so dried it was useless for food or planting.

senses.1: Dried up, withered, or hardened through desiccation, describing grain in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:23). The seven ears of grain were 'thin and withered,' blasted by the east wind until they dried to uselessness. The Aramaic connection to 'stone' suggests they became hard as rock. In the dream's interpretation, these withered ears symbolized seven famine years that would devastate Egypt, grain so desiccated it could neither feed nor seed.

gloss_terse: Zaanan, a town in Judah's Shephelah
gloss_readable: This place name identifies a town in the Shephelah (lowlands) of Judah, appearing in Joshua 15:37. It may be the same location mentioned in Micah 1:11 as Zaanan (or Tzenan). The Septuagint renders it Senna or Sennam. As part of Judah's territorial allotment, it was one of the lowland towns between the coastal plain and the hill country, strategically positioned in the fertile agricultural zone.

senses.1: A town name in the Shephelah district of Judah (Joshua 15:37), possibly identical with the Zaanan of Micah 1:11. Located in the lowlands, it was part of Judah's western territory. The Septuagint preserves the name with Greek adaptations. Though no events are specifically associated with this town in Joshua, its inclusion in the boundary lists establishes it as part of the tribal inheritance, a settlement in the productive lowlands.

gloss_terse: to walk humbly, conduct oneself with humility
gloss_readable: This verb in the Hiphil infinitive absolute means to walk humbly or conduct oneself with modesty. Micah 6:8 uses it in the famous summary of God's requirements: 'to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God.' The intensive infinitive form emphasizes the ongoing nature of humble walking. The root suggests being reserved or modest, the opposite of pride. This isn't occasional humility but a continuous posture of modesty before God.

senses.1: To walk humbly or conduct oneself with modesty, appearing in Micah 6:8's triad of divine requirements: 'act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God.' The Hiphil infinitive absolute intensifies the meaning—making oneself walk humbly, cultivating humble walking as a practice. This goes beyond isolated acts of humility to a sustained manner of life, characterized by modesty, self-effacement, and awareness of one's place before God. The multilingual evidence confirms the humility sense.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes humble or modest persons, appearing in Proverbs 11:2 in contrast to arrogance. The verse states, 'with the humble is wisdom,' while pride brings disgrace. The plural form designates those characterized by modesty and self-effacement rather than presumption. This is not weakness but proper self-assessment, the quality of those who don't overreach their knowledge or position. Wisdom gravitates toward such humble people, avoiding the arrogant.

senses.1: Humble or modest in character, describing people who practice self-effacement. Proverbs 11:2 contrasts 'the humble' (with whom wisdom dwells) with 'the arrogant' (who receive disgrace). The adjective marks those who have a proper, modest view of themselves, neither claiming undue importance nor overestimating their knowledge. This humility creates space for wisdom—the teachable heart that can receive instruction, unlike pride which thinks it already knows.

gloss_readable: This noun appears to mean winding, wrapping, or possibly a turban, found in Isaiah 22:18. The context is God's judgment on Shebna, with imagery of wrapping and tossing like a ball. The exact meaning is debated—some see it as a turban or wrapping cloth, others as the act of winding. The root verb means to wrap or wind, so this noun likely denotes either the wrapped object or the winding action itself.

senses.1: A winding, wrapping, or wound object (possibly a turban), appearing in Isaiah 22:18's judgment oracle against Shebna. The difficult passage involves imagery of wrapping and hurling: God will 'wind you tightly like a ball and throw you into a large country.' The noun from the root 'to wind' may refer to the act of winding or to something wound (like a turban). Either way, the image is violent containment followed by forceful ejection.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes a jar or container, appearing in Exodus 16:33 where Moses commands Aaron to 'take a jar and put an omer of manna in it' for preservation before the Lord. This was to be kept for future generations as testimony. The Targum suggests a basket, but context and other versions support 'jar'—a vessel suitable for long-term storage of the preserved bread. The specific container type mattered for this memorial function.

senses.1: A jar or pot used for storage, specifically mentioned in Exodus 16:33 for preserving a sample of manna. Moses instructs Aaron to 'take a jar, put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept for the generations.' This container needed to preserve the bread as a permanent witness to God's wilderness provision. The jar became a memorial object, eventually placed in the ark's vicinity (Hebrews 9:4 tradition).

gloss_terse: pipes, channels (for conducting oil to lamps)
gloss_readable: This masculine plural construct noun refers to pipes or channels, appearing in Zechariah 4:12 in the golden lampstand vision. The prophet sees 'two golden pipes' that empty golden oil from the olive trees to the lamp. These channels conducted oil from source to light, sustaining the flame. The formation involves an inserted 'ת' according to Hebrew grammar patterns. The image emphasizes continuous supply—the pipes ensure unending flow from divine source to illuminating function.

senses.1: Pipes or channels that conduct liquid, specifically in Zechariah 4:12's vision of the golden lampstand: 'the two gold pipes that pour out golden oil.' These channels connect the olive trees to the lamp, ensuring continuous oil supply. The pipes represent the means by which divine empowerment (oil symbolizing the Spirit) flows constantly to enable Israel's light-bearing mission. Without these channels, the lamp would empty; with them, supply is perpetual.

gloss_terse: armlets, ornamental bands for the upper arm
gloss_readable: This noun refers to ornamental bands or armlets worn on the upper arm, listed among women's jewelry in Isaiah 3:20. Some translate 'ankle chains,' but the better interpretation is armlets that clasped the upper arm. These were luxury items, part of the elaborate finery the prophet condemns. Scholars suggest reading this word also in 2 Kings 11:12 (for the textual 'testimony'), meaning royal armlets placed on Joash at his coronation. The jewelry marked status and wealth.

senses.1: Ornamental armlets or bands worn on the upper arm, mentioned in Isaiah 3:20 among ladies' luxury items. While some translate 'ankle chains' (from the root for 'step'), the better view is arm ornaments that clasped the upper arm, visible markers of wealth and status. These decorative bands were part of elaborate feminine finery. Textual proposals suggest royal armlets in 2 Kings 11:12, making them insignia of royalty as well as feminine adornment.

gloss_readable: This place name appears in 2 Kings 8:21, where Joram crosses over to Zair (or Zairah in Hebrew form) to fight the Edomites. The location is uncertain, likely somewhere on or near Edom's border. The Septuagint renders it Seior or Sior. The narrative context is Edom's successful revolt against Judah—Joram went to Zair, was surrounded by night, broke through, but ultimately failed to suppress the rebellion. The exact site remains unidentified.

senses.1: A place name associated with Edom's region (2 Kings 8:21), where King Joram fought against the Edomites during their revolt. The location is uncertain, probably near Edom's border. The Septuagint suggests connection to Seir. In the narrative, Joram 'went over to Zair' with his forces but couldn't quell the rebellion despite a nighttime breakout from encirclement. The name marks a battlefield in Judah's unsuccessful attempt to retain Edomite vassalage.

gloss_readable: This noun means youth or the state of being younger, appearing in Genesis 43:33 where Joseph's brothers are seated 'according to birthright and according to youth'—oldest to youngest. The construct with suffix means 'according to his youth' or 'in order of his being younger.' This systematic seating by age astonished the brothers since the Egyptian official (secretly Joseph) had no apparent way to know their birth order. The noun captures relative youth or position as younger.

senses.1: Youth or younger status, used in Genesis 43:33 to describe the seating arrangement of Joseph's brothers: 'according to his birthright and according to his youth'—meaning from oldest to youngest. The precise age-ordered seating amazed the brothers, since this 'Egyptian' shouldn't know their birth sequence. The noun emphasizes relative position in the age hierarchy, the state of being younger rather than absolute youth, fitting the context of comparative ranking.

gloss_terse: parched, dried out from thirst or heat
gloss_readable: This adjective intensifies the idea of being completely dried out, going beyond ordinary thirst to extreme desiccation. Isaiah uses it to describe people so parched with thirst that they are dying (Isa 5:13). The Spanish 'reseca' captures the sense of thorough drying, while the English 'parched-of' shows the construction with the following noun.

senses.1: Describes the state of being extremely dried out or desiccated, especially from lack of water. Isaiah 5:13 depicts the exile's severity: people 'parched with thirst,' showing complete dehydration. This intensive adjective form (note BDB's citation of Gesenius §84b-c) emphasizes the extremity of the condition, not merely thirsty but utterly withered.

gloss_readable: This verb describes brilliant whiteness or dazzling appearance, particularly of skin. The Syriac cognate suggests brightness and clarity, while the Aramaic points to polishing. In Lamentations 4:7, it describes the Nazirites' radiant appearance before Jerusalem's fall—their skin 'more dazzling than milk,' whiter than snow. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'eran blancos,' English 'bright') confirms this sense of brilliant whiteness.

senses.1: To appear dazzlingly white or brilliant. Lamentations 4:7 uses this to describe the Nazirites' complexion before the siege: 'more dazzling than milk,' parallel to 'whiter than snow.' The verb emphasizes radiant, gleaming whiteness rather than mere color, suggesting skin that shone with health and vigor in contrast to their later emaciated state.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes land that has been scorched or parched by heat. The root suggests extreme dryness, beyond what rain can relieve. Psalm 68:6 uses it to describe the desolate places where God settles the rebellious. The Spanish 'sequedad' and French 'terre desséchée' both capture the sense of thoroughly dried earth, land too parched to support life.

senses.1: Land that is scorched and dried to the point of desolation. Psalm 68:6 describes God making rebels dwell 'in a parched land,' suggesting barren desert as both geographical reality and divine judgment. This goes beyond normal aridity to describe earth burned and hardened, inhospitable to human habitation.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a repulsive odor, particularly of decay. Joel 2:20 uses it in parallel with another word for stench to describe the smell of the invading northern army when God drives it away. The doubling of stench-words ('his foul smell' parallel to 'his stench') emphasizes the complete putrefaction of the defeated horde. French 'puanteur' directly captures this sense of repulsive smell.

senses.1: A foul, nauseating smell, especially of rotting organic matter. Joel 2:20 depicts God's judgment on the invading army: 'his foul smell will rise up,' paralleled by 'his stench.' The imagery suggests corpses decomposing in the sun, a graphic picture of total defeat. The Siracide reference (11:12) also uses it for offensive odor.

gloss_readable: This plural noun describes areas of extreme drought or scorched land. Isaiah 58:11 uses it in God's promise to satisfy His people's needs even in the driest places. The root connects to scorching heat and parched ground. The Spanish 'sequías' (droughts) and the broader context of divine provision in waterless places show this refers to regions where water is desperately scarce.

senses.1: Scorched or drought-stricken regions where water is absent and the ground is parched. Isaiah 58:11 contains God's promise: 'He will satisfy your needs in scorched places,' assuring provision even in the most barren environments. This builds on the root idea of land dried by intense heat, emphasizing not just aridity but the burning, scorched quality of the terrain.

gloss_terse: reddish-gray, tawny (of wool or possibly a place name)
gloss_readable: This noun appears to describe either a color of wool or possibly a place name. The primary sense is reddish-gray or tawny wool mentioned in Ezekiel 27:18's catalog of Damascus's trading goods. Some scholars suggest it might be 'wool from Zahar' (a location), though this is disputed. The color term fits the context of luxury trade items, while translations vary between 'white' (Spanish, French) and the more technical 'tawny' suggested by BDB.

senses.1: A reddish-gray or tawny color, specifically describing wool in the luxury trade of Damascus (Ezekiel 27:18). The exact shade is debated—BDB suggests 'tawny' or 'reddish-gray,' while some translations opt for 'white.' The multilingual evidence shows uncertainty, but the context of fine trade goods suggests a distinctive, valuable color of wool, possibly from a specific region or processing method.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes the color of donkeys, appearing only in Judges 5:10 in Deborah's song. The root relates to colors in the reddish, tawny, or light spectrum. The phrase 'you who ride on tawny donkeys' addresses the wealthy or ruling class, since lighter-colored donkeys were apparently prized. Spanish 'blancas' (white) and the English retention of 'tawny' show the range of interpretation, but the sense is clearly a desirable, distinctive coloring.

senses.1: Describes a tawny or light coloring of donkeys, suggesting animals of higher value. Judges 5:10 addresses 'you who sit on tawny donkeys,' apparently referring to leaders or the wealthy class. The specific color marked status or breeding quality. The root connects to reddish-gray or tan hues, distinguishing these animals from common darker donkeys.

gloss_readable: This plural noun refers to those who hunt, derived from the root for hunting or trapping. Jeremiah 16:16 uses it in a striking metaphor: God will send first fishermen, then hunters to seek out the exiled Israelites. The hunters represent the thoroughness of God's pursuit—no hiding place will suffice. The multilingual glosses uniformly render it 'hunters,' confirming the straightforward occupational sense.

senses.1: People who hunt or trap animals, used metaphorically in Jeremiah 16:16 for divine agents pursuing scattered Israel. God declares He will send 'many hunters' to search out His people from every hiding place. The image suggests relentless pursuit and thorough searching, moving beyond the fishermen's nets to the hunters' tracking skills in mountains and rocks.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes an instrument of punishment and public humiliation, likely a wooden collar or stocks that restrained prisoners. Jeremiah 29:26 mentions it alongside 'stocks' as tools for restraining mad prophets. The context shows it was used by authorities to control and shame those deemed troublemakers. Spanish 'argolla' (ring, collar) points to the restraining function, while the parallel term confirms it was a device for physical constraint.

senses.1: A restraining device, probably a collar or pillory used to punish and publicly shame prisoners. Jeremiah 29:26 describes the temple officer's authority to put any madman who prophesies 'in the pillory and collar,' showing it was paired with stocks for maximum restraint and humiliation. The device both restricted movement and marked the wearer as condemned.

gloss_terse: Zior, a town in the hill country of Judah
gloss_readable: This proper noun identifies a town in the hill country near Hebron, listed among Judah's inheritance in Joshua 15:54. Modern identification places it at Ṣâʿîr, about five miles north-northeast of Hebron according to Buhl's geography. The Septuagint renders it variously as Σωρθ or Σιωρ. The multilingual glosses preserve the name in transliteration, reflecting its status as a geographical designation.

senses.1: A town name in the tribal allotment of Judah (Joshua 15:54), located in the hill country region. Geographical sources identify it with modern Ṣâʿîr near Hebron. The name appears in the territorial lists defining Judah's inheritance, one of many settlements in the central highlands that formed the tribe's core territory.
